# Sharp projective energy versus actual centroidal retained volume

Let K be a convex body in R^d, d>=1, and y in int K. Define the ordinary
projective volume energy

 E_K(y)=inf_a integral_K[1+a.(x-y)]^(-d-1)dx,             (1)

where the denominator must be positive on all of K. Define the largest
dominated mass having barycenter y by

 T_K(y)=sup{integral_K f dx: 0<=f<=1,
                         integral_K(x-y)f(x)dx=0}.       (2)

The zero density is permitted, but the optimum below is positive.

**Theorem.** Both optima are attained. The energy minimizer is unique.
The retained-mass optimum is an indicator of ONE actual convex cap of K
with centroid y (the whole K if y is its centroid). In particular it is
also the largest volume of a convex subbody of K with centroid y. Exactly

                    T_K(y)<=E_K(y)<(d+1)T_K(y).          (3)

The lower equality holds if and only if y=g_K. The constant d+1 in the
upper inequality is optimal, although no compact body and interior point
attain it. A simplex with y approaching a vertex supplies the exact
limiting ratio d+1.

This is an ordinary theorem. In particular its sharp conversion loss
is d+1; it does not turn a mixed base-energy lower bound M/2^n into OC.
The cap construction differs from the archived base-moment realization:
here the continuous centroid itself is prescribed and maximized mass
is attained by its hinge dual's cap.

## 1. The retained mass is attained by a centroidal cap

Translate y to zero and write V=|K|. Consider the finite convex function

                 G(u)=integral_K(1+u.x)_+ dx.            (4)

It is coercive. Indeed K contains a ball rB centered at zero, and

 G(u)>=integral_(rB)(u.x)_+ dx=c(d,r)||u||,

where c(d,r)>0 is independent of u. The last equality follows by rotation
and scaling (and holds directly for an interval when d=1). Therefore G
attains its minimum at some u*. It is C1: at u!=0 the cutting hyperplane
1+u.x=0 has Lebesgue measure zero, and bounded difference quotients are
dominated by ||x||; at u=0 every denominator is positive in a neighborhood.
Dominated convergence also gives continuity of the derivative. Thus

       grad G(u)=integral_(K intersect {1+u.x>=0})x dx.   (5)

Let D=K intersect {1+u*.x>=0}. It has positive volume and contains a ball
around zero, since zero is interior to K and strictly satisfies the cut.
Stationarity gives integral_D x dx=0. Consequently

              G(u*)=integral_D(1+u*.x)dx=|D|.            (6)

For every feasible f in (2),

 integral f=integral(1+u*.x)f(x)dx
              <=integral(1+u*.x)_+dx=|D|.               (7)

The actual indicator 1_D attains this bound. This proves directly,
without an unproved infinite-dimensional duality assertion, that

 T_K(0)=|D|=min_u G(u).                                  (8)

Every convex subbody with centroid zero is one feasible indicator, so
the same D is the maximum-volume such subbody.

If g_K=0, take u*=0 and D=K. If g_K!=0, every minimizing u* is nonzero
and gives a proper cut: otherwise its captured set has full volume and
the moment in (5) equals Vg_K!=0. Thus both the cap and its complement
have positive volume, and its cutting plane meets int K. Equality in
(7) forces f=1 on the positive side and f=0 on the negative side,
almost everywhere. Hence the maximizing density is unique a.e. and its
convex cap body is unique. Two different proper cutting planes would
give different indicators on an open subset of int K; hence the
normalized u* is also unique in this noncentroid case. Uniqueness of u*
is not asserted in the centroid case, where all sufficiently small u
give the same full cap.

## 2. Energy attainment and the exact lower equality case

For completeness, the admissible energy parameters form the bounded
open convex set Omega={a:1+a.x>0 on K}. The inner ball gives ||a||<1/r.
The energy has positive definite Hessian

 (d+1)(d+2) integral_K xx^T(1+a.x)^(-d-3)dx.              (9)

It tends to infinity on the boundary of Omega. To see this, let a_j tend
to a_0 on that boundary and take x_0 in K with 1+a_0.x_0=0. Let delta_j
=1+a_j.x_0 tend to zero. A fixed small (d-1)-disk E in a_0-perp around
zero lies in the interior ball. The cone conv(x_0,E) lies in K. At
(1-t)x_0+t v its volume element is a positive constant times t^(d-1)dt dv,
and its denominator is at most delta_j+C t. Integrating only over
delta_j<=t<=2delta_j gives a lower bound c/delta_j tending to infinity.
For d=1 the disk is a point and the same interval calculation applies.
Thus the energy minimum is attained uniquely inside Omega. The facts
also appear, with the escort identities, in
`candidate 5811f0ad1132ce56`.

For every L>0, convexity of L^(-d-1) at L=1 gives

 L^(-d-1)>=[1-(d+1)(L-1)]_+,                            (10)

with equality only at L=1. At the minimizing a, integrate (10) and
use (8) with hinge parameter u=-(d+1)a. This proves E>=T. If a!=0,
then L!=1 outside a hyperplane of zero volume, so the integrated
inequality is strict. If a=0, energy stationarity says g_K=0; conversely
g_K=0 makes a=0 stationary and optimal. In that case E=T=V. This proves
the lower equality statement in (3).

## 3. A centroidal-cap section comparison with an infinite cone

Assume d>=2 and g_K!=0. Use the proper cap D from Section 1 and put

 s=1+u*.x,  B=d+1.

Let phi(s) be the coarea-normalized section-volume density, so

 integral_K F(1+u*.x)dx=integral_a^b F(s)phi(s)ds           (11)

for every nonnegative Borel F. Explicitly phi is the section's H_(d-1)
measure divided by ||u*||. Its support is the finite interval [a,b],
with a<0<b. Its (d-1)st root is concave on (a,b), by actual parallel
section inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski; the constant coarea factor does
not change that property. Extend phi by zero outside [a,b]. The cap
mass and centroid equations are exactly

              integral_0^b phi=T,
              integral_0^b s phi=T.                     (12)

First b<=B. Choose a point of D at height b. For 0<=t<=b, its homothety
of D with ratio 1-t/b has all heights at least t and has volume
(1-t/b)^d T. Thus the height survival function of uniform D is at least
(1-t/b)^d. Integrating gives its mean at least b/(d+1). The mean is one
by (12), proving b<=d+1.

Define the comparison density on the entire half-line s<=B by

 psi(s)=c(B-s)^(d-1), c=dT/B^d;
 psi(s)=0 for s>B.                                      (13)

Its restriction to [0,B] has the same mass T and first moment T as phi.
The following two precise comparisons hold:

 phi(s)<=psi(s) for every a<s<0,                         (14)

 integral_0^B w(s)phi(s)ds<=integral_0^B w(s)psi(s)ds
             for every finite convex w on [0,B].        (15)

Here and below point values at support endpoints have no integral role.

Proof of the two comparisons. On the actual projection interval the
function

 h(s)=phi(s)^(1/(d-1))-c^(1/(d-1))(B-s)

is concave. Because b<=B, the set on (0,B) where phi-psi is positive
is an interval: inside (0,b) it is the positive superlevel interval of
h, and outside (0,b) the difference is nonpositive. If phi and psi
agree a.e. on [0,B], they have the same root on (0,B), and concavity
extends h(s)<=0 to s<0. This proves (14), while (15) is equality.

Otherwise the matched two moments imply that the positive interval is
nonempty and has endpoints 0<r_1<r_2<B. For example, if it started at
zero, then (s-r_2)(phi-psi)<=0 everywhere, strictly on a set of positive
measure, contradicting the zero mass and first-moment differences.
The case where it ends at B is the reversed argument. Thus phi-psi
has the signs nonpositive, positive, nonpositive across these endpoints.
Its root difference at zero is nonpositive by continuity (zero is an
interior section), and it is positive at some s_0>0. Concavity on the
segment from any a<s<0 to s_0 then gives h(s)<0: explicitly

 0>=h(0)>=[s_0/(s_0-s)]h(s)+[-s/(s_0-s)]h(s_0).

This proves (14). For (15), let ell be the affine line joining
(r_1,w(r_1)) and (r_2,w(r_2)). Convexity gives w<=ell between the
endpoints and w>=ell outside. Therefore (phi-psi)(w-ell)<=0 pointwise.
The integral of ell(phi-psi) vanishes by the two matched moments.
Integrating proves (15). This argument requires no smoothness of phi,
no optimizer over bodies, and no unproved localization theorem.

## 4. The sharp upper constant

The particular energy parameter a=-u*/B is admissible, because

       1+a.x=(B+1-s)/B>=1/B>0 on K.                     (16)

Use the convex positive kernel w(s)=(B+1-s)^(-d-1), finite on [0,B].
Equations (14)--(15), and phi=0 below its finite lower support endpoint,
give the STRICT comparison

 integral_all phi(s)/(B+1-s)^(d+1)ds
       <integral_(-infinity)^B psi(s)/(B+1-s)^(d+1)ds.   (17)

Strictness follows already on (-infinity,a), where phi vanishes and
psi is positive; all other comparison contributions have the correct
sign by (14)--(15). The cone integral is finite and elementary:

 integral_(-infinity)^B psi(s)/(B+1-s)^(d+1)ds
   =c integral_0^infinity t^(d-1)/(1+t)^(d+1)dt
   =c/d=T/B^d.                                         (18)

The last equality follows from the substitution r=t/(1+t), leaving
integral_0^1 r^(d-1)dr=1/d. Multiplying (17) by B^(d+1), and evaluating
the admissible parameter (16), proves

                      E_K(0)<B T_K(0).

If y=g_K, this upper inequality is immediate from E=T>0 and B>1.
This proves (3) in every d>=2.

## 5. Intervals and the sharp simplex family

For d=1, translate y to zero and write K=[-l,r] with l,r>0. The maximal
centroidal interval is [-m,m], m=min(l,r), and the hinge certificate in
Section 1 makes its length exactly T=2m. Direct integration and
minimization, or the simplex calculation below, give

 E=4lr/(l+r),
 E/T=2 max(l,r)/(l+r) in [1,2).                          (19)

Thus the interval case has the same sharp constant d+1=2 and equality
at the lower end precisely at the midpoint.

Here is an exact all-dimensional sharpness calculation. Let

 K=conv{0,e_1,...,e_d}, V=|K|=1/d!,
 y=(epsilon,...,epsilon), 0<epsilon<=1/(d+1).

Its barycentric coordinates are lambda_0=1-d epsilon and
lambda_i=epsilon for i>=1. More generally, for any simplex and interior
barycentric coordinates lambda_i, its projective energy is

             E=V(d+1)^(d+1) product_(i=0)^d lambda_i.    (20)

To prove (20), write w_i=v_i-y. Specify the positive affine denominators
L_i=1/[(d+1)lambda_i] at its vertices. Since sum lambda_i L_i=1, these
are the values of one affine denominator 1+a.x in the translated
coordinates, positive on the whole simplex. The map x->x/(1+a.x) has
Jacobian (1+a.x)^(-d-1), and sends the simplex to the simplex with
vertices w_i/L_i. Its centroid is zero, since
sum_i w_i/L_i=(d+1)sum_i lambda_i w_i=0. By change of variables this
centroid equation is precisely the energy stationarity equation.
Strict convexity therefore certifies this parameter as the minimizer.
The transformed simplex has volume V/product_i L_i: in its augmented
vertex determinant, multiply each column by L_i and subtract a times
the first d rows from the last row, restoring the original augmented
vertex matrix. This proves the claimed volume ratio and (20).

For the displayed y, the actual cap

              D={x in K:sum_i x_i<=(d+1)epsilon}

is the homothetic simplex (d+1)epsilon K and has centroid y. It is not
merely a convenient feasible subbody: the normalized hinge cut
1+u.(x-y)=(d+1)-sum_i x_i/epsilon has this exact positive region, and
its derivative is the zero moment of D. Thus (8) proves that it is the
maximal retained centroidal cap. Hence

 T=V(d+1)^d epsilon^d,
 E=V(d+1)^(d+1)(1-d epsilon)epsilon^d,
 E/T=(d+1)(1-d epsilon).                                 (21)

As epsilon decreases to zero, the ratio increases to d+1. At
epsilon=1/(d+1), y is the original centroid and the ratio is one.
All bodies here remain compact; the upper sharp constant occurs only
as the selected interior point approaches the vertex. If d=0 is
desired, the sole convex body is a point and E=T=1 under H_0, separately.

## 6. What the comparison does and does not retain

The theorem gives an ACTUAL convex cap centered at the prescribed y
with mass T>E/(d+1), and the loss d+1 is unavoidable. It is stronger
than merely rescaling the escort density to be bounded by one, but it
does not preserve the escort law or its individual cap masses.

The finite-base zonoid comparison and integer-centerpoint lower bound
in `candidate 2b7d1c7e003a98d0`
are different measures and constraints. Applying this ordinary theorem
fiberwise requires actual prescribed points in those fibers and cannot
turn a base-only energy number into an ordinary volume. No cross-fiber
compatibility, mixed halfspace bound, or general OC conclusion is inferred.
